abstract: Nanoflow liquid chromatography coupled to mass spectrometry (LC-MS) has become central to low-input and single-cell proteomics (SCP), where trap-and-elute workflows offer sample loading flexibility and analytical column protection but introduce additional dead volume, surface area, and a largely uncharacterized trade-off between flush direction and chromatographic performance. Here, we present a systematic, iterative benchmarking study of a purpose-built family of NanoShield trap columns against the established PepMap Neo trap cartridge and direct injection. Using a standardized workflow built on a commercial HeLa digest standard, we evaluated performance across two mass spectrometry platforms, multiple LC gradient lengths, both flush directions, and a range of sample input amounts and injection volumes. Shortening of the NanoShield packed bed, from an initial 5 cm format to a 1.2 cm format, closed a substantial sample loading time penalty and largely eliminated a pronounced forward-flush performance deficit, while remaining superior to the PepMap in reverse-flush mode and approaching direct injection level identification numbers, peak width, and quantitative precision. A next-generation NanoShield featuring a stationary phase with larger pore size further narrowed the residual forward-flush penalty. These results demonstrate that trap column bed length and stationary phase chemistry are key, partially independent design levers for closing the performance gap between trap-and-elute and direct injection workflows, and provide practical, present-day guidance for trap column selection and operation in low-input proteomics.
